opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's tricky, because you're not really comparing apples to apples. A fine-tuned model, say a BERT-style model trained specifically on sentiment data, does exactly one thing. You give it a movie review and it gives you "positive" or "negative," maybe a probability score, and that's it. It's small, it's efficient, and it was built for that exact task.

A multitask or general-purpose generative model works very differently. You prompt it with something like "Is this review positive or negative?" and it generates text. Sometimes it says "positive." Sometimes it says "This review expresses a mostly positive sentiment, although..." and goes on for a paragraph. So even measuring accuracy requires decisions: how do you map free-form output back to a label? Do you constrain the output? Each choice changes the results.

Then there's the efficiency side, which is what I really care about. The generative model is doing so much more computation for the same answer. It has many more parameters, it generates tokens one by one, and output length varies, so the energy per query isn't even stable. In our experiments, using a big general-purpose model for something like sentiment analysis could cost far more energy than a small task-specific model, often for similar or even worse performance.

The training story is also hard to untangle. The fine-tuned model has a pretraining cost plus a fine-tuning cost. The multitask model has a huge upfront training cost that's supposedly amortized across all the tasks it can do. How do you attribute that cost to sentiment classification specifically? There's no clean answer.

So the comparison depends heavily on your setup choices. But I think it's an important question to ask, because there's a trend now of using these huge generative models for everything, even when a much smaller, purpose-built model would do the job just as well at a fraction of the cost. People should at least be aware of that trade-off when they choose a model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that came up a lot when we were doing the energy and carbon comparisons across models. The intuitive thing to do is say, okay, here's a model that was fine-tuned specifically for sentiment classification, like a BERT or a DistilBERT fine-tuned on SST-2, and here's a big general-purpose model that can also do sentiment classification if you prompt it. Let's compare them on the same task. And on paper that sounds like a fair comparison, because the output is the same: positive, negative, maybe neutral.

But the problem is that they're not really doing the same thing. The fine-tuned model has one job. It takes a sentence, it produces a label, and that's the entirety of what it can do. The multitask or zero-shot model is doing something fundamentally different. It's generating text. It has to parse your instruction, figure out that you're asking for sentiment, and then produce an answer in natural language, which you then have to post-process to turn into a label. So even for a single example, the computational path is completely different, and the amount of compute, and therefore energy, is often an order of magnitude or more higher for the general model. That's one of the results that really stood out to us: the gap between a task-specific model and a general-purpose model doing the same classification was huge.

And then there's a second layer, which is how do you even attribute the cost? With the fine-tuned model, you have training on the base model, plus fine-tuning, plus inference, and you can roughly account for all of that. With a multitask model, the training cost is amortized across potentially hundreds of tasks, and nobody knows how to split that up. Should sentiment classification get one hundredth of the training emissions? One thousandth? It depends entirely on how the model gets used downstream, which we don't know at the time we're evaluating it.

There's also a question of what counts as the task. For a classifier, accuracy on a benchmark is pretty well defined. For a generative model, you're also implicitly evaluating prompt design, decoding strategy, how you map free-form outputs back to classes. If the model says "this review seems a bit mixed but leans positive," is that right or wrong? So you end up comparing two systems that have different inputs, different outputs, different cost structures, and you're squashing all of that into a single number. And that's what makes me hesitant. It's not that the comparison is meaningless, it's that the number hides more than it reveals, and if you don't document all those choices, people take it as apples to apples when it really isn't.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the classifier’s label output with the multitask model’s ability to generate natural-language, free-form answers.

astra-6.text:
It’s difficult because even if you give them the same sentiment classification examples, they don’t necessarily approach the task in the same way. A fine-tuned model has been trained specifically to map an input to a set of labels, like positive or negative. With a multitask model, you’re often describing the task in a prompt and asking it to generate an answer. So the wording of the prompt, and how you interpret that answer, become part of the comparison.

You can compare their accuracy, but that doesn’t isolate the effect of fine-tuning versus multitask training. You’re also comparing different model sizes, training data, and ways of producing an output. It’s hard to make that an apples-to-apples comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it’s hard to make it an apples-to-apples comparison. A fine-tuned model has been trained specifically for sentiment classification, usually on examples from the same dataset you’re evaluating it on. A multitask model is trying to do a whole range of things, and you might be asking it to classify sentiment just through a prompt.

So if one performs better, what are you actually measuring? Is it the benefit of task-specific training, the size of the model, or how well the prompt works? Even the output is different: one model gives you a label, while the other generates text that you have to interpret as a label. You can compare their scores, but those scores don’t tell the whole story.
